utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated. We are here now to hold a Status Conference, and I am proposing an agenda which will take up the same agenda items as we had at the previous Status Conference. Today we are going to discuss the use and admission of prior statements of witnesses, the use and admission of photographs, the defence of alibi, the Judges' questions; we're going to raise the question of depositions and, in a certain sense, the question of timetable, and any other questions that may arise, depositions by Presiding Officers. I would like to tell you that we would like to cover all the points on the agenda; that is, if we need to continue in the afternoon, we shall do so because we really must resolve all these matters to ensure the proper conduct of what I call the administration of justice and justice itself. I think that our highest interest is the interest of justice, and the administration of justice is just a way of organising the road to achieve that supreme goal. So we come to the first point: the use and admission of prior statements by witnesses. I wish to share with you a few ideas which are just questions for discussion. As you know, there are different types of documents that can be considered as prior statements in the sense of Rule 66 of the Rules of Procedure. For the needs of this discussion, we will make a distinction between three different types of statements: statements made to the Office of the Prosecutor, statements made to other official institutions; namely, those of other countries, statements made at hearings within the framework of other trials, which one could call transcripts. So we're going to discuss these matters in general, and afterwards we will have specific matters to rule on. The discussion should first focus on the first type of statements, that is, prior statements made to the Office of the Prosecutor. The question that arises in connection with the use of such statements affect, among other things, the principle of orality of debates and the possibility of questioning or challenging the witness statements and, more broadly, the credibility of the witness. In other words, the Prosecutor, if we caricature a little certain proposals made, can he limit himself to confirmation by the witness of the totality of the prior statement and asking the admission of the same. The Defence in that case would be in a position to conduct a cross-examination solely, or almost solely on the basis of a written document. Of course, I repeat, I'm caricaturing things a little. Vice versa, in the hypothesis that the Prosecutor goes into a detailed examination-in-chief, should the Defence have the possibility to use the prior statement, risking that that statement may contain elements that have not been touched upon by the Prosecution and which the Defence may consider prejudicial for his client; or should the Judges use only abstracts of that statement, risking the possibility of dealing with them out of context and without being able to verify them by examining the totality of the text; or do the parties imagine that the Judges should base their opinion on the testimony at the hearing and the whole prior statement of a witness? Finally, the Chamber notes that the defences of various accused in this case seem to have divergent views regarding the use of statements, that is, whether they should be used in their totality or partially, or not used at all. The parties should have met yesterday afternoon to discuss this matter. What are their observations? Have they reached an agreement? That would be a good question. Furthermore, what are the other types of prior statements, specifically the transcripts? Regarding the latter, should we not consider that when they are public, then everyone, that is, the parties and the Judges as well, can refer to them without necessarily having them admitted as exhibits, having them admitted into evidence? These are a few questions which the Chamber would like to share with the parties so as to have a fruitful discussion. According to the order I have suggested, I will begin with Ms. Hollis or Mr. Niemann, I don't know which of you would like to speak, and then I will give the floor to each Defence counsel. Ms. Hollis.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Prosecution will address the points that you have raised. Before doing so, the Prosecution would suggest that the definition of statement may be broader because we look at the statement in terms of both parties, not just the Prosecution. And we suggest that if a witness has provided something in writing to either party and adopts that as their own, then that could be considered as a statement so that the Defence also would have available to it in its case, the use of statements. But now turning to the classifications that Your Honour has set forward. In terms of the Office of the Prosecutor -- well, first of all, in terms of orality challenging the statement and challenging the credibility, we suggest that credibility can be assessed even when one party used statements because the other party will cross-examine. We also suggest that very often, a statement would be offered as part of the evidence and the witness would indeed be called upon to provide additional oral testimony regarding the case. Credibility of a witness is not limited to attempted impeachment by inconsistencies in statements. Both sides investigate these witnesses. There are other modes of impeachment such as using other witnesses to indicate that this witness told a different story to them. That would not be impeachment by a prior statement that is offered to the Court. Pointing out contradictions in the statement and other evidence, so that the use of statements would not preclude the opposing party from impeaching the credibility of a witness. We agree that it is important that the witness come forward and be present in the courtroom, and wherever possible that should be done. We suggest the use of statements does not preclude that happening. Every one of these witnesses will be here in the courtroom and will be subject to cross-examination. If there is no cross-examination, we suggest that's because the other party doesn't oppose anything the witness said. So that we believe that orality can be met by bringing the witness forward as we would do in virtually all cases, but it would not deprive the opposing party of examination orally in the courtroom. We note that some of the rules allow for situations where a witness would come forward, their statement would be put into evidence. That is allowed for in terms of expert witnesses. We suggest that in terms of the principles we are talking about here today, there's really no difference in those procedures. We also note that there is some procedure whereby an affidavit or formal statement of a witness can be introduced even without the witness being present. So again, we suggest that that would be a contrary argument to the position the Defence is taking about our suggested use of statements because that's allowing statements to be used even when a witness is not here. Now, in terms of statements of the Office of the Prosecutor, we suggest, as with all statements, what is important is that the witness adopt those statements. We suggest that it would be better for the Judges to have the entire statement or, at a minimum, to have all parts of the statement that refer to the matters that are disputed, but our position is it would be better for Your Honours to have the entire statement. We do not have jury trials here, these are judge alone trials. Your Honours are able to review those statements and determine what is relevant to you in making your determinations at trial, and our Rules of Evidence indicate that anything that is relevant and has probative value is allowed into evidence here. We suggest it would be up to Your Honours to determine the relevance and the probative value and assign the weight accordingly. So we would suggest that you should not only be given abstracts but should be able to give with the statements in context. We also suggest that the judges should be able to base their opinion on both oral testimony and the entire prior statement when it is used. Perhaps we should make a clarification here. We are not suggesting that parties be forced to introduce prior statements into evidence. We are suggesting they be allowed to do so when they believe those prior statements are relevant and would assist the fact-finder and would expedite the proceedings. In terms of prior testimony, we believe that that is, perhaps, another form of statement. Your Honour, I believe, has mentioned it as another form of statement. Prior testimony before this Tribunal, we believe, should be allowed into evidence where it is relevant and probative. In that regard, the Prosecution's position is that the Trial Chamber should consider no evidence in making its fact-findings unless that evidence is formally admitted at trial, because if it's not formally admitted at trial, then how, on appeal, can the parties determine what the Trial Chamber actually relied upon? So we agree that public testimony is in the public domain, but we suggest that the Trial Chamber should not use such public testimony unless it is offered into evidence. And in making that statement, we realise that the Judges themselves may call for additional evidence. We believe it should be formally introduced into evidence. Regarding statements to other official institutions. Again, we believe that if a party puts that statement forward as relevant and probative, and Your Honours agree, and the statement is adopted by the witness in court with or without corrections, we suggest that that statement should be admitted into evidence and that Your Honours should determine the weight to be assigned to such a statement. Your Honour, I believe I've covered all of the questions that you raised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I have a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Do I take it from your categorisation of these things that your position doesn't go as far, or tell me if I misinterpreted it, it doesn't go as far as to say that if you have a statement, be it an OTP statement or another institutional statement, and the witness isn't available for cross-examination and we're not in a 94 ter situation, which is covered by the Rules but is fairly well circumscribed as to what it can be. If we're not in that situation, do you -- you would not be advocating that you could just put in a witness statement without the witness being here and if it didn't fall into 94 ter, are you?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution would not advocate that as a general rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: We believe that if a party would be able to put forward sufficient circumstances to justify it and sufficient reliability for the statement, perhaps, but certainly not as a general rule, no, Your Honour. Perhaps a witness makes the statement and then the witness dies and it is relevant to the matter. But these are abstract, and I think they'd have to be dealt with on a case-by-case basis and we believe that would be in very limited circumstances. But as a general rule, no, we're not advocating the use of those statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: And the second question I have is that when you talked about the entirety of a statement coming in when it's been introduced originally as part of an impeachment process of the witness, you don't think as we've seen in -- I'm not sure this trial, but certainly in some trials, where you'll have a long witness statement of seven or eight pages, the Defence counsel, could be the Prosecution, but the Defence counsel seeks to show an inconsistency in one paragraph of that statement and many times, the witness will have covered events in the statement, some events that should not even have been touched upon in the main testimony at hand. But you really do think that we, the Judges, have some power that allows us to assess the reliability of a couple of written paragraphs that haven't even been touched upon by the main witness ahead of us, or you would suggest in that -- because we went into this a little bit the other day, you would suggest in those circumstances we could start asking the witness all over again about stuff that was in the -- that she or he hadn't covered before that was in that statement? I mean I have some scepticism on this, as you can tell.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I note your scepticism. First of all, we would be of the opinion that in such a circumstance, if the party then sought to introduce the entire statement, the other party would be allowed to question on that. If it is something that is not relevant to these proceedings, we believe that either Your Honours could order that that be deleted or that Your Honours could disregard it because Your Honours are Judges who are chosen for your experience, and we believe you could disregard it. If it is relevant to issues before Your Honours, we believe that it would be admissible into evidence, again with an opportunity for the opposing party to touch on it. So our bottom-line position on all these statements is that the question is, are they relevant and are they probative to issues you have to decide, and if they are, we suggest they would be admitted. And then how the opposing party would deal with those could either be to put on the record they believe certain portions are not relevant to this trial or not probative or to go back and question regarding those items.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: You don't see any problem with the Article in the main ICTY Statute about confronting your accusers. I know you have the witness there, but if you've got something in the statement the witness hasn't even mentioned and you just have the statement there.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: If the witness is there and it's the witness' statement, then the opposing party is able to confront the witness about what is in that statement. We believe that's what is meant by "examine" or "have examined" the witnesses against you, and that is the language of the Statute, of course. Many people equate that with confrontation. If there is a difference, at least the plain language of the Statute is to examine or have examined the witnesses against you, and we believe that the opposing party would have an opportunity to examine on those matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Let me give you one last example. I don't want to use up all the time. You are the Prosecutor, as indeed you are. You put the witness on the stand and you ask the witness about incidents A and B. The Defence counsel then puts in, in order to impeach the witness on something he or she said about incident A, they put in a statement. The statement contains not only information about incidents A and B about which the witness has been questioned, but incidents C, D, E, and F. Do you think that you, the Prosecutor -- and you may not be entirely happy with what the witness said in the statements about incidents C, D, E, and F -- do you think you, the Prosecutor, can then take up and start questioning the witness who's here sitting in the stand about incidents C, D, E, and F, or that we have this great power of discerning from the written statement the reliability of that?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, in your scenario, it is our statement but it is the Defence who introduces these other ones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: We believe, then, that we would be allowed to question the witness about those incidents. It is our statement. I think in many jurisdictions you can impeach your own witness even. I think very often if, as you may say so, we're not entirely happy with what's in the statement, but if that's what the witness said, that's what the witness said, but we would be allowed, I think, to explore that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Hollis, I should like to follow up this reasoning of Judge Wald. Imagine that neither the Prosecution, and therefore the Defence either, because the Defence is limited by the limits of the examination, so neither the Prosecution nor the Defence are questioning about events D, E, F, et cetera, but the Judges see that these are important incidents for a determination. Would you agree that the Judges should take up those incidents or not? I have my own opinion but I should like to learn yours.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Well, certainly, Your Honour, in this practice, Your Honours can ask questions and ask for additional evidence. If Your Honours believe that this is relevant and it is probative and would assist you in reaching decisions in the case, we believe that you could question the witness. Your question, Your Honour, we suggest, goes into others we'll be discussing today, and that is what is the appropriate and allowed response of the parties should Your Honours do that? But the Prosecution's position is that Your Honours can ask questions about any matters that are, to you, relevant and probative and would assist you in making your decisions in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We're now going to hear the Defence regarding these points, and then we will go on to the next agenda item. Mr. Krstan Simic. I'm sorry, Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence has agreed that Mr. O'Sullivan will be speaking on behalf of Mr. Kvocka's, Kos', Prcac's, and Zigic's Defence, whereas Mr. Fila will be speaking on behalf of the Defence team of Mr. Radic, and that is why Mr. O'Sullivan was on his feet. But I should just like to say a few words before that. We discussed a topic yesterday regarding the proceedings themselves and time was limited and I wasn't allowed to say what I had to say, so I should like to go back to that question and say what I have in that regard. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, but I didn't quite understand your point, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Last time when we started the Status Conference, we talked about the course of the proceedings. Ms. Hollis spoke and it was my intention to raise a matter at that time, but as the time was limited to five minutes -- you asked me if I could complete within five minutes and I said no -- you said that we could continue today. I'd just like to bring your attention to that question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. As you know, in the agenda we have an agenda item called "miscellaneous" or "other matters," so we'll come back to that then. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. As Mr. Simic has stated, I will be making submissions on behalf of Kvocka, Kos, Zigic, and Prcac. Your Honours, I will respond to your questions and to the Prosecution. I also intend to bring to your attention two decisions of this Tribunal, one Trial Chamber decision and one Appeals Chamber decision, which I submit support our position. What is our position? It is this: We say that the use to which prior statements can be used in these proceedings is limited -- the question of admissibility is limited. By "prior statements," we include all the types of statements Your Honour has identified. We submit that the admission of a prior contradictory statement to impeach a witness is admitted for the limited purposes of demonstrating the impeachment and is not admitted to establish the truth of the contents of that statement. Your Honours, under the legislative framework of this Tribunal, I submit that the cases to which I will refer support our position. On this matter, there is one Article and two Rules which are germane to this issue, that is, Article 21(4)(e) of the Statute, Rule 90, and Rule 85. Let's turn to the Rules first. Rule 90(A) is very short and it states as follows: "Subject to Rules 71 and 71 bis, witnesses shall, in principle, be heard directly by the Chambers." The two exceptions, Rule 71 refers to depositions and Rule 71 bis refers to videolink. The central issue, therefore, in our submission, is the meaning to be ascribed to the words "testimony of witnesses." We submit that testimony of the words of a witness given under oath or affirmation in these proceedings. "To give evidence" or "to be heard," in our submission, means that the person appears in court, testimony is extracted from that witness and used in these proceedings. Rule 85(B) reflects that procedure I have just described whereby there's examination-in-chief, cross-examination, re-examination, if any, and Your Honours' questions, if any. That, I submit, is the general framework under the Rules. Rule 90 and 85 reflect the rights guaranteed to the accused under Article 21(4)(e). That provision is very short and I'll read it to you: "It's the right of the accused to examine or have examined the witness against him and to obtain the attendance and examination of witnesses on his behalf under the same conditions as witnesses against him." What are the rights guaranteed to an accused, as a minimum guarantee in full equality? In answering that question, we rely on this decision: It's the decision on the motion to allow Witnesses K, L, and M to give testimony by means of videolink conference. That's a decision from the case of the Prosecutor versus Delalic and others, decided on 28 May, 1997. The issue in that case was whether the right of the accused, under Article 21(4)(e), was violated when a witness gave testimony via videolink. The Trial Chamber ruled that that right was not violated. Can I direct Your Honours' attention to paragraph 15 of that decision, and I will quote briefly from that passage. The Trial Chamber said this: "It is important to reemphasise the general rule requiring the physical presence of the witness. This is intended to ensure confrontation between the witness and the accused, and to enable the Judges to observe the demeanour of the witness when giving evidence. It is, however, well known that video conferences not only allow the Trial Chamber to hear the testimony of a witness who is unable or unwilling to present their evidence before the Trial Chamber at The Hague, but also allows the Judges to observe the demeanour of the witness whilst giving evidence." The Chamber went from there to say that the right was not violated. In our submission, the following propositions follow from this decision and the interpretation of Article 21(4)(e). The first proposition is this: The right to confrontation. The right of the accused to be confronted with a witness against him. The right to a face-to-face meeting with the witness appearing before the trier of fact. A right to hear what the witness has to say. The second proposition is this: Demeanour. Your Honours must observe the demeanour of the witness when he is testifying. You must observe outward appearance and behaviour, facial expression, tone of voice, gestures, willingness or hesitation in answering questions, all questions. The third proposition is this: Credibility. Credibility, the quality which makes evidence worthy of belief. As the fact finders, you have a duty and obligation to observe this behaviour and draw your conclusions on the issue of credibility. Hearing and observing a witness throughout the witness' testimony ensures fairness and integrity of the proceedings. When a witness comes into court with a splitting headache, holding an ice pack and placing it on his forehead, a fair and impartial fact finder stops the proceedings. I submit that's to ensure fairness and integrity. The second case I wish to draw to your attention is the Tadic appeal judgement of 15 July 1999. One of the grounds of that appeal brought by the Prosecution successfully was whether the Defence could be ordered to disclose to the Prosecution the witness statement of a Defence witness after that witness had completed examination-in-chief. The appeals Chamber said that the Prosecution may apply for such disclosure following examination-in-chief of a Defence witness, and the Trial Chamber has the power to make such an order. What I submit is clear and implicit in that decision is that witnesses are intended to testify in direct evidence viva voce. Witness statements are to be used for cross-examination. Witness statements are certainly not admissible for the truth of their contents nor can they be tendered as such. There appears to be a certain inconsistency, Your Honours, in the Prosecution position. When we discussed this issue last week, the Prosecution was suggesting that witness memory may have faded since the time the statement was made. Well, if we accept that proposition, it amounts to this: We are precluded from conducting a cross-examination. If the witness cannot answer cross-examination because his memory has faded, and they're offering a statement for the truth of its contents, we can neither cross-examine the witness or the statement. The Prosecution takes the position that our Rules do not preclude what they are proposing. To the contrary, I submit the Rules do preclude it and the jurisprudence of this Tribunal clearly sets that out. Rule 94 ter is immaterial to this question. Affidavits are used in corroboration of other people's testimony so it does not apply. We've had questions about the expert. I recall Judge Wald asked me whether there was a sharp distinction between what appears to be the accusatory expert. Well, if it's true that at times a witness appears accusatory, I submit that the expert should be brought up to the level of the fact witness which is to say all witnesses should be heard directly on examination-in-chief. The Prosecution relies on Rule 89(C) by saying that these statements may be relevant and probative. We say they are inadmissible under 89(D). Rule 89(D) states that a Chamber may exclude evidence if it's probative value is substantially outweighed by the need to ensure a fair trial. In my submission, this is clearly a case where 89(D) would make these out-of-court statements inadmissible. Your Honours, we were in week five or six of this trial when this issue arose at week five or six of this trial. The Prosecution is asking to you move the goal posts mid-stream. The Prosecution is asking you to reduce the notion of examination-in-chief to a nonsense, to make it meaningless. They're asking the witness to take the stand, adopt a statement on the basis of one or two leading questions, and say "There, there's your examination-in-chief. Now go ahead and cross-examine that person." This makes the notion of examination-in-chief meaningless. Therefore, our position is as follows: As I said, out-of-court statements, as Your Honour has defined them are admissible for the limited purposes of showing impeachment, if any, for Your Honours to weigh and assess credibility, and they are not admissible for the truth of their contents. Your Honours have an obligation to supervise proceedings, to uphold the rights of the accused, and to strictly apply the statute and the rules as they are set out. Unless I can be of further assistance to you, those are my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I have one question which may be a repetition of our discussion last week, but in order to keep this record fairly complete, let me ask it again. In your argument that Article 21(4)(e)'s rights are impugned if the witness who is here, sitting in the stand, is not required to give complete testimony by oral evidence, and yet that's a harder proposition, at least for me to accept if the witness is, in fact, right there and you, the Defence counsel, can ask any questions you want. You can go right down the whole list and repeat, I suppose, every question in the statement, should you so choose. Then why aren't you fully accorded -- your clients fully accorded their rights to confront the accusers and we have ability to see the demeanour. You could, if you wanted, and I assume you accept this, if you didn't think it was worth your while you could, say, stipulate to the Prosecutor and say, "Look, the first half of that statement was fine with us, we'll let it in," right?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: We could, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I mean you always had that right even though it might cut back on our ability to see the demeanour of the witness in full. So why isn't the basic core of the right of your confrontation protected as long as the witness is sitting there and required to answer any question that's relevant that you'd put on cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: In my submission, it goes to the nature of statements taken by one of the parties to a dispute. The importance of the confrontation in cross-examination, in my submission, must occur when the statement is made. If we look at the continental system where the investigating magistrate is there with the witness, Prosecution, and Defence at the time of making that statement, there's an independent body taking a statement, the confrontation can occur at that moment. And that's what can't occur when we have a statement taken by a party to the dispute, not knowing what the questions were, how they were put, how the witness reacted. That's unfair to the fact finder. It's unfair to the accused. Your Honours, we have these two major legal systems, and I've glossed over the continental system, and there are people here who know that much better than I do, the continental system, and I fail to see why in the year 2000, in an international court, we are trying to abandon both the history and practice that we are familiar with in the common law and the safeguards that we are familiar with in the civil law to come up with something which is untried and fraught with problems and unfairness. I submit we should not embark on that journey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. O'Sullivan, I still have a little question for you. All that you have said in relation to the rights of the accused, the credibility, the observation of the witness and so on is linked to the principle of orality and all this is valid under the hypothesis that there is no agreement between the Prosecution and the Defence, am I right?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: By agreement and stipulation to certain facts; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: With the stipulation to facts, there's no need to bring them out in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but I have another question. For those stipulations, as you said, in that situation, how can I put it, can one envisage, in relation to transcripts from other cases, can we imagine the possibility of stipulations because I see that you have included all prior statements, though we did make a distinction as regards transcripts from other cases, but you have included all in one under the same category. From your personal point of view, is it possible to have stipulations regarding the admission of the whole transcript and have the witness appear only in cases when the Defence wishes to cross-examine?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Not only would I agree with that, I would welcome it. And it seems to me that, I believe it's Rule 65, talks about the parties to agreeing to certain matters of law and fact, and on top of that, we have judicial notice, adjudicated facts. So I agree with Your Honour. Where there is agreement, that should by all means be pursued.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. O'Sullivan. Mr. Fila next. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours, for taking up part of your time but I should like to assist, if I may. In order to answer the questions in the order you put them, I shall begin by quoting an example. There is a witness whose name is Idriz Mujkic; he lives in Australia. He was a detainee in Omarska. In conversation with him, we came to the conclusion that he would testify to the advantage of the accused Radic -- on behalf of the accused Radic. Mr. Niemann, as you know, lives in Australia. I asked him to take that statement; Mr. Niemann did take the statement, and in conformity with Mr. Niemann, I shall tender it into evidence without calling the witness. Why, in a situation of this kind, would I have to bring the man all the way from Australia? That is one example of how this matter can be settled. The other point is the following: A statement, Your Honours, has several items taken by one of the parties: There are the general basic information, particulars, then you have the background information, and then you have the time from when the witness stepped into Omarska itself. Now, why would it be necessary to ask the witness on the first two parts of that? Can't we agree that the former witness, for example, is truly a retired seamstress? So that means saving a lot of time. What we cannot agree on is that somebody should be deprived the right of cross-examination, and that is, in fact, the case that has happened during this trial; that is to say, if a witness statement is tendered into evidence, admitted into evidence, in the additional questions asked by the Prosecutor, because then do not have the right to respond in cross-examination. So in a case of that kind, and that is something which happened before this Trial Chamber: that one of the counsel mentioned that statement and then Ms. Hollis, in her additional questions, asked that this be an exhibit, in her re-examination. The statement made negative mention, for example, of my own client and I no longer can have the right to ask any questions, to re-cross-examination because it has not gone through the examination-in-chief. Then that would not be a fair trial and the rights of the accused and the Defence counsel would have been infringed upon. In the Dokmanovic case, for example -- I don't want to go through it all, it has all been published -- this matter was solved very simply by Mr. Niemann and myself, we dealt with it very easily by placing certain restrictions, limitations. A statement cannot be adopted as evidence without the presence of the witness unless we agree that that can be so. If, in the examination-in-chief, or during the cross-examination, on the other hand, the difference is raised as to the difference in the written statement and his testimony in court, if there is a difference and discrepancy between the two, then we will uphold what has been said in the testimony in the courtroom and eliminate the previous statement. Finally, we always agreed that the statements be adopted and accepted. If you look at the statements which are eight pages long, for example, the different sections might be matters of interest to us, and it is that section which is interesting and important for our part of the story. So your decision will not be influenced by the fact of whether the witness was a retired seamstress or librarian or whatever but whether she was abused, maltreated, beaten, and who the perpetrators of that were. Therefore, personal particulars, the background, there's no need to present that here before the Court unless somebody has acquired any new knowledge and information in the matter; for example, that the witness has changed his address, his place of residence, or a new child has been born to him, or anything of that kind. So statements cannot be tendered in additional examination but straight away, and then we can see what we can agree on, the points we can agree on before the proceedings. Any point being contested must be the subject of both the examination-in-chief and the cross-examination. Then that is a fair and equitable trial and each party's rights have been upheld, and we have tried and tested the witness on the key issues, the key points. That is all I wanted to say. Thank you. Just one moment. I do apologise. As far as the transcript is concerned of previous trials, the transcripts of previous trials and the statements made there by witnesses, they are public documents and they cannot be eliminated, or ignored, for that matter, but I do agree with Ms. Hollis that you must quote them if you're going to use them. You must mention them if you're going to use them for us to be able to enter into polemics on that basis, but they cannot replace the witness unless we agree to do so, of course. That speeds up the whole process, and it speeds it up quite considerably. Therefore, where I agreed with Mr. Niemann was under the Presiding Judge, Judge Cassese, and that is what I explained to you in the Dokmanovic trial and none of the parties were infringed upon. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I just have one question of clarification, Mr. Fila. Under the system that you would like to see adopted, say the Prosecution had a witness statement and they would submit it in advance, or you had it already, and then you would --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have it too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Yes. You would look at it and you would say, "Well, we're not worried about what's in the background of the witness or even in the events leading up to Omarska, but we are worried about anything that's said about the conditions in the camp," and then at that point, I just want to get this straight, you would tell the Prosecution you want the witness when the witness comes to be examined directly on Omarska, as well as cross-examined, not what I think Ms. Hollis would like which is to tender the statement, including some parts of the conditions at Omarska, and then just have you cross-examine. I just want to make sure I understood your proposition. You would say, if you contest it, you want to have direct testimony as well as cross from the witness directly; right? Okay. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, Your Honour, in any points that are being contested. For example, if something extraordinary happens and somebody comes and says that Krkan's shift was the best shift, I would of course be surprised and astonished but I wouldn't object to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fila, I also have another question for you. From the practical point of view, could one, in your opinion, could the Defence, within a reasonable time limit, say to the Prosecution -- after receiving the statement and having it in your hands, would it be possible to underline the parts which you are ready to stipulate and learn what would be contested? And then the Prosecution could prepare in advance and could tender that statement already marked by you, for instance, and then the object of the examination-in-chief and the cross-examination would be only the parts that were not underlined. What would your comments be regarding this practical procedure, from your standpoint?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, that is precisely what I want. That is it in a nutshell. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Perhaps we shall give Ms. Hollis a chance to respond, and then once again to the Defence. Ms. Hollis, do you have any observations to make?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honour. Of course, in regard to your last point, we would suggest that we don't need to have their stipulation to offer the testimony. However, on a practical note, we would suggest that if you have one accused and one Defence counsel, that that may be a very expeditious way to proceed; when you have five accused and ten Defence counsel, which one of the underlinings do you go forward with and not go forward with? Now, that's a practical aspect that doesn't deal with the principle you are putting forward. In regard to Mr. Fila's submission, he indicated to you that regarding transcripts from previous trials, well, you could use those but they couldn't replace the witness. Well, Your Honour, in the Aleksovski case, that's exactly what happened and the Appeals Chamber upheld that. A transcript from a prior trial was introduced by the Defence. Now, the Prosecution's objection was that they wanted the witness called and in large part for the purposes of cross-examination, because it's not just the accused who has the right to examine the opposing witnesses, it's either party. But the Appeals Chamber said not only could the transcript be used but that the Prosecution didn't really have the right to cross-examine that witness. Now, they did allow the Prosecution to put in the statement of another expert but that expert was never called either. So, indeed, in the evolving practice of this Tribunal, you can put in a prior transcript, you don't have to call the witness, and the other party, in some instances which we suggest should be very rare, if existent at all, the other party may not have the right to even call that person and examine them. So opposing counsel didn't cite that case when they were citing jurisprudence that may be relevant. We suggest that that is the most on-point to what we are dealing with here. In respect of the Celebici case, we suggest that that is not on point and we suggest that the language there cannot be construed to say you can't use a prior statement, because Defence counsel is saying that the opportunity to observe the demeanour and to cross-examine means they have to give oral testimony only. We have stated repeatedly that that's not our position; that you can observe demeanour based on cross-examination, you can observe demeanour based on your own questions, and cross-examination can take place on prior documents. In regard to the Tadic appeal judgement, that is not on point either. It was not a question of whether the Defence could use statements, it was a question of whether if they called a witness to testify and they had taken a prior statement from that witness, could the Prosecution have the benefit of that prior statement to determine if there were any inconsistencies. So it was not the same issue at all and, we suggest, is not really instructive on this point. Regarding a witness losing their memory and thus depriving the Defence of cross-examination, we suggest that if a witness has made a prior statement and at that time they had a memory, and now many years later they come into this court, would it not be true that the interest of justice should at least allow that that statement be introduced if the witness adopts it? And would not their current loss of memory, many years after the event, be a matter of what weight, if any, the Judges were to attribute to the prior statement? We suggest that perhaps there's some merit to that consideration. The Prosecution is not trying to change things in the middle of this trial. With our very first witness we raised the issue of using prior statements in the form of prior testimony. We had discussed before that the use of statements in this trial. So contrary to Mr. O'Sullivan's assertion, we are not, at a late moment, trying to change the Rules. We raised this point very early on and we are now at the point where perhaps we can have a determination on this issue. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Hollis, I have a question raised by your comments. You mentioned the Aleksovski case and I should like to ask you your opinion regarding this question. How do you see the transcripts from another case in the light of Rule 94 ter, that is affidavits? That transcript, does it have anything to do with an affidavit, could it be compared or are they two quite different things? What is your opinion, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution would think that there could be a technical distinction between prior testimony and an affidavit. Now, 94 ter has been an amended to also include a "formal statement". Perhaps prior testimony would be closer to a formal statement. But we would suggest that 94 ter would unduly restrict the use of prior testimony because we believe the plain language of that Rule states you can only use this affidavit or formal statement to corroborate other evidence about facts at issue. We suggest you can use it as direct evidence in the trial. So that would be our response regarding 94 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Ms. Hollis, if we are supposed to construe, as Mr. O'Sullivan suggested, sort of all the Rules, try to make them act in tandem with one another and you start out with Rule 90 saying in general, in general, we're going to have live testimony, and then you say, except for deposition, you can use that and if you file certain things, and you can use judicial notice if you file with certain Rules, and 94 ter is for the affidavit evidence for collaboration with notice ahead of time, and in accordance with the law of the -- what is the use of all of those if you can then jump all of those and just go straight to a kind of Rule 89(C) type things which says, listen, the court, any time it thinks anything is probative and reliable, even if it's an affidavit or a transcript or a statement before that, if it thinks it's useful, it can use it. I mean what it's like, you know, driving the old, you know a hole that you can drive a truck through.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, if I could attempt to respond to that Your Honour. Your Honour, I would suggest that there has been an evolution in these Rules. And if we look at the Rules, for example, if we look at the Rule that says, in principle, witnesses will testify live. It cites two exceptions but, in fact, there are four exceptions today, and one of those doesn't even require the witness to be present. So we would suggest that, indeed, if you read those as a whole what does it come down to as a core question and that is the right, in particular, of the accused, but we suggest the right of both parties to be able to examine the evidence against them. The real question here, we suggest, is how do you define that? And we suggest that if a witness is here ready to be examined, that is, examining the evidence against you and the matter of how their evidence comes to you in terms of the party presenting that witness, then we suggest that there is room for an evolution of that, both to expedite the proceedings to truly try to proceed in the interest of justice where people are talking many years after the fact, yet have made earlier statements that they will adopt in the courtroom. The opposing party is here to cross-examine. Your Honours are professional judges who can assign weight according to the all the circumstances that come forward. So we suggest as long as this basic principle, being able to examine the evidence against you is adhered to, and as long as the witnesses are brought to the greatest extent possible that, indeed, if you read the framework as a whole that could be consistent. Because from the very beginning there have been countless amendments to these Rules to deal with circumstances that this Tribunal faces. The bottom line is a fair trial to both parties. We believe that our suggested use of these statements would not deprive either party of a fair trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. O'Sullivan. And I apologise, but I would like you to consider this question: It is true that there is a whole series of rights of the accused which we must respect. But one of the rights of the accused is an expeditious trial, and we know that there must always be a balance between expeditiousness and fairness. So everything we are talking about, prior statements, the need to always have a witness in person, to cross-examine him, to see him physically, except for exceptions, would that not impinge upon the principle of an expeditious and fair trial at the same time?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: The short answer to your question is, in my submission, it would not the overriding consideration here in the trial. Based on what we say is the proper construction of the Rules and the practice in this Tribunal. There were three very brief points I'd like to respond to. First, the Aleksovski appeal decision. If there is a case that does not apply to this circumstance, it is the Aleksovski appeal decision. In that case, we were talking about expert witnesses, and the Defence expert from the Tadic trial whose testimony was used in Aleksovski was rebutted by the Prosecution expert from Tadic in Aleksovski talking about events in the Lasva Valley on the issue of international armed conflict. The second point is this: In regards to memory, I raised that point with Your Honours earlier because at the last Status Conference, Ms. Hollis said it. She said at page 2682 of the transcript, "Why should we force witnesses to go forward on the basis of their current memory when they have given prior statements? What did we learn from that? We learn that memory fades over time." So it was her point not mine. But if she's correct, as I pointed out earlier, I submit there's a problem. The witness will say, "My memory is not as fresh as it was," so on the basis of a statement, I can't cross-examine the witness and I certainly can't cross-examine the statement. And lastly with Rule 90, Ms. Hollis is quite correct, there are two exceptions to Rule 90 within Rule 90. All the other exceptions fall outside Rule 90. They are not testimony. Those are my submissions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fila, do you have any final observations to make, no? I think we shall think over this point and we will render our decision. So we can now go on to the second agenda item, the use and admission of photographs. Questions arose when two types of photographs were used. Mr. Fila, I see you are on your feet. Do you want to say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it is also the quality of the photographs that is in question and the way in which they are presented. The photograph might have been shown, taken from another angle of an individual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fila, can you let me finish, please? I am just opening the discussion here. I was saying, there have been questions posed regarding the use of two types of photographs. And if I don't cover the whole issue, you will have a chance to do so. For example, a photograph showing injuries, others showing different persons. For instance, this is an example, generally speaking, photographs come under the same Rules as the other exhibits and are therefore admissible within the bounds of Rule 90 of the Rules of Procedure. It is up to the parties to contest the admission of such a document, to make a showing that they are not pertinent or that their admission do not conform to the principles of a fair trial. To facilitate the discussion, it would be desirable that the parties producing photographs should also supply all information about origin, date, and the objects they show. It would also be necessary that the parties should be particularly careful when persons are entailed to avoid any direct or indirect challenge to the identity. Madam Prosecutor, regarding the photographs of bodily injuries, can you respond to the objections of the Defence or will you withdraw your submission for their admission?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we can respond to the objections. As the Prosecution recalls that there were two objections to the photograph which was 3/31, and the objection, I believe, was by Defence counsel for accused, Radic. The first objection was he had no idea where this was taken or the circumstances. We point out to you that 3/31 was included in our list of exhibits and it does indicate that it is a photograph of the bruises on a person by the name of Jakupovic and the photograph was taken by Dr. Idriz at Trnopolje. So indeed in the index it did indicate where the photo was taken, who was in the photo, and by whom. Secondly, the objection was that the photograph didn't show accurately injuries because Defence counsel indicated he had never seen a person who looked like that. Your Honour, the photograph was shown to the witness and the Prosecution recalls that the question to the witness was, "Does this photograph show the types of injuries you observed on detainees at Omarska?" And the witness indicated yes, the photograph did show the types of injuries the witness had seen on detainees at Omarska. We suggest, Your Honour, that when a photograph is used in that way, it really doesn't matter who it is in the photograph, when it was taken or by whom. The relevance is what is depicted on that photograph is consistent with the kinds of things the witness saw at the named location. So we suggest that, indeed, that photograph should be admissible. If the Defence has questions of the witness about were the bodies really that red or the bruises really that black, they can pose those questions to the witness. But the witness has told Your Honours that, indeed, what was shown on that photograph was consistent with what that witness observed on bodies of detainees at Omarska. That is how we would respond to that photograph. In terms of single photographs of individuals who may be suspects, I believe that's what Your Honour was talking about, where identity may be an issue, is that -- I believe that's what you were talking about, the Prosecution is certainly aware that where accused are still named in our indictments and yet we do not have them in custody or if we have them in custody but identity is in dispute, that a single photograph shown to witnesses would potentially have problems in terms of any identification that was made and any weight that could be assigned, the single photographs that have been shown in the courtroom have not been of persons who remain as accused in cases before this Tribunal. But we are cognisant of that issue and the fact that we could be jeopardising identifications if we used single photographs for people. If Your Honours have no questions, those would be my comments on photographs as evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Ms. Hollis. The Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for interrupting you, Mr. President, I thought you had opened the debate. The first thing I wanted to say was that I did not see the original of the document at the time. It was a poor copy of a document where the man seems to be red like a red Indian, if I may use that comparison, and he was particularly red on his shoulders. So there is no Slav that is as red as that, except perhaps when he's sunburnt. The danger of using poor quality photographs, and photographs taken from another location is that it questions our intelligence. Do we know what injuries look like? Should I now bring you from Belgrade all the bodies, the dead bodies that I've seen in the course of my practice, and I've seen many thousands, and whether dead people looked like that, the ones that were aligned around the "white house". So this is bringing somebody's intelligence into question. If we're talking about a bruise, we know what a bruise is, but if you have a man who was in Omarska and you have a photograph of that injury and wound on that particular person, then that is relevant to Article 5 of the Statute and that's another story and I have nothing against that, of course. I'm not contesting that at all. But this is Trnopolje. Some man, who knows who it is. It's a poor-quality photograph. I don't mind if you adopt that, it won't make any difference to me, but I think it's useless, a useless exercise, and it just shows that we don't know what a bruise looks like and we need the witness to tell us that a bruise is, in fact, what is shown on the photograph, which, as I say, is a poor-quality one at that. That's all I wanted to say. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fila, you spoke on behalf of all Defence counsel, or only in your own name? All right, then. Thank you. Ms. Hollis, any comment?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honour. Does it really question the intelligence of the people in the courtroom to look at a picture like that? How many people have seen bruising that is that deeply black? How many people have seen that degree of bruising on a body? So to show the degree and the seriousness of the mistreatment of prisoners in these camps, we suggest, is very relevant to see what these people would have looked like. Secondly, Your Honour, we're talking about people here that the Prosecution has alleged are the leadership in the camp, and one of the things is did they know what was going on so that they could interfere? If you see a person who has deep black over his kidneys and bruises and cuts on his body, should you take notice of that if you're a leader? It's relevant to issues in this case, Your Honour. So we suggest that, indeed, not everyone has seen bruising that severe or that widespread on a body and that it is relevant to issues that you have before you here. We suggest it does not insult your intelligence but, we believe, would assist the fact-finder in making determinations here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I spoke about a photograph where you can see a red man with something even redder on his back. I didn't see a photograph with cuts, with something black on it. Take a look at the photograph in question. And another thing, it is just a poor-quality photograph. It's a copy, it's a photostat; it's not the original, and that is an insult to my intelligence, and that is the experience and practice of all of us. We've all seen bruises but we ought to see bruises from Omarska. If you ask someone about that, then you should be showing that, and then if you show something red, you can't say that it was black. What you have just received is something red on red with something even redder, and on the person's back at that. That's what I was talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fila, I have this question for you: I know that that may be an insult to your intelligence because I know that you're very intelligent, but there is something else. Mr. Fila, we are delivering justice for the benefit of the public too who are not so familiar with these things like we are. But if you think about the public, do you think that that photograph may be useful or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my legal system, the Trial Chamber has in all its competencies, and I'm sorry that you do not have those competencies. I do not want to deprive public opinion of the possibility of seeing the inhumane conditions which, let me repeat, I say did exist in Omarska. But I think that the photograph must be an original so that you can see what Ms. Hollis is referring to, and not a witness to be asked to look at a poor-quality photograph and say, "Was it like this? Is this what it looked like?" and I think that it should be stated that this is not a photograph from Omarska, et cetera. Let us take it the other way round. You could take it from forensic medicine textbooks, because we all had to pass a forensic medicine examination, at least in our system. You have all manner of photographs, so why shouldn't Ms. Hollis resort to a medical textbook, a forensic textbook, and refer to injuries and wounds contained in those textbooks? And then she can ask the witness whether he or she saw injuries to that effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too. To clear up a point, when I said to show to the public, it's not in order to make a show of it but from the standpoint of justice. We can close the discussion on this point too and proceed to the third point or third item of the agenda, that is, Judges' questions. As you know well, the Judges have the right to conduct the debates to ensure the best justice and the best administration of justice, the distinction that I have already made today regarding the order of the presentation of evidence, in accordance with the provisions of Rule 90, all the powers incumbent upon it from Rule 98 to request additional evidence or to call additional witnesses. It is therefore natural for the Judges to put questions to a witness. One can say this to address all the questions that we discussed today regarding the common law and civil law system. We have gone beyond that stage and we are now talking about the Tribunal system itself. In exceptional cases, the Judges speak only after the parties have completed their examination-in-chief, their cross-examination, and, if any, re-examination, in order to clear up and present their points of view. As you know, Rule 95(B) says, at one point, that the witness is first questioned by the party calling him, but Judges may also ask any questions of the witness at any stage of the proceedings. We have come to an agreement in the Chamber that if there is a point that needs to be clarified straight away, we may intervene -- of course Judges can ask questions at any point of time -- but we have agreed to ask questions preferably after the questions of the parties, because after all, the parties should be given the opportunity to put their questions to the witnesses, and at the end, the Judges will put theirs. At the end of that procedure, it is assumed that the parties have exhausted the questions that they had for the witness. It appears, therefore, except in the case of clear error, for example, regarding the name of a town or a person, or lapses, the party should not take the floor again whereby they would be running the risk of entering into polemics between the Judges and one of the parties, which would be contrary to a good administration of justice. On the other hand, it is up to the parties to present any opposing arguments either by bringing in other witnesses or by presenting their submissions in the course of their rebuttal case or in their written or oral submissions. All that I have said is a question open for discussion. Have you any observations to make regarding what has been said? My question is first addressed to the Prosecution. Ms. Hollis.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, certainly the Prosecution is aware of the Rule that allows Your Honours to ask questions and we believe that that Rule is a very wise one and allows Your Honours, who are the fact-finders in the case, to ask any questions necessary to clear up matters in your own mind. The Prosecution would suggest, however, that an opportunity be given to the parties following questioning by the Judges to ask if the parties have any follow-up questions that are raised based on the questions Your Honours have asked. We believe that this would be a very limited sort of questioning, but we believe there could be instances where either party would have follow-up questions. Certainly this counsel's personal experience in the Tadic case was that the Judges asked questions -- they were very actively involved, as Your Honours are -- and then at the conclusion of their questions, they asked each party if any party had questions based on what the Judges had asked. So we would suggest that that is a possible procedure that could be very closely guarded by Your Honours but that anything coming up in the course of your questioning that hadn't been covered earlier, the parties would have the right to do so. We would not disagree with the Defence, in principle, that if a question is asked which appears to be contrary to the testimony, that perhaps the party can raise concerns about that. The Prosecution is not at all sure that a party can object to what a Judge does, but perhaps if a party has a concern about the content of a question, they could raise their concerns at that moment so that Your Honours would be aware that perhaps the transcript isn't exactly as you thought it would be. The reason the Prosecution believes that this could be of assistance to you is that as trials go along and transcripts become several thousands of pages in length, it's sometimes difficult to go back and pick up each one of those instances and clarify it later. Your Honours, that would be the Prosecution's submissions on this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is there anyone to respond on behalf of the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, on behalf of the Defence teams, Mr. O'Sullivan will be taking the floor, but Mr. Fila reserves the right after Mr. O'Sullivan's address to make his own statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you, Mr. Simic. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: First of all, I'm happy to report that we did discuss this with the Prosecution beforehand and we find Ms. Hollis' suggestions extremely reasonable, and the follow-up questions may be an avenue to pursue depending on the nature of the, for lack of a better word, objection or point of clarification. As far as the second proposal, it may indeed be the result of a lacunae in the Rules, the way in which a party brings to the attention of a Judge what that party considers to be a misformulation of what the witness said. Again, I agree with what Ms. Hollis has suggested. When this issue first arose several weeks ago, I mentioned Rule 5 objections because there was no other basis to bring this to the attention of the Trial Chamber. So there's, perhaps, room there for improvement in the Rules. But in the meantime, if we can adopt a procedure by which we voice our views, because we are, after all, required to create a record both for these proceedings and any subsequent proceedings. So there must be a mechanism for all parties to raise these matters with the Chamber. Those are my observations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. O'Sullivan. Mr. Fila, do you have any additional remarks?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, not to what has been said. But I should just like to give an explanation and apology to Judge Riad. The whole thing began by a comment -- that is to say, Judge Riad quoted the witness as saying something in a different manner than the witness actually said, and I made a comment. I did not say that the witness did not mention Krkan's shift as being the worst. The remark by the Defence, and it can be seen on the transcript at page 2274, relates to a single word there, one single word, and the word was "cruel" or "svirep" in our language. In one of your languages, it is "cruel" in French or "cruel" in English. "Cruel." Judge Riad used the words "most cruel" because he was speaking in English on the occasion, and I reacted to that and said that the witness did not, in fact, use these two words, "most" or "cruel" or "plus cruel" in French. Why? Because I did not wish to hurt Judge Riad in any way, offend Judge Riad in any way, and if I did offend him, I should like to offer my deep-felt apologies. That was not my intention at all. In my own country's Criminal Code, you have the category of murder, and then you have the category of cruel murder. The difference is in the death sentence penalty. Each murder implies a certain dose of violence. For murder proper, we provide a sentence ranging up to 15 years' imprisonment. If the murder was committed in a cruel manner, if it is termed a cruel murder or especially cruel, or whatever, then the death penalty can be invoked. That is the sole reaction, my sole reaction in saying that the witness, on page 2338 and 2339 did not use the word "cruel." If I offended Judge Riad in any way, I do apologise. But I just wanted to say that the witness did not state that, and that is what I wanted to say by way of explanation and apology.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I just want to thank Mr. Fila and tell him that I appreciate very much his intervention. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Hollis, do you have any additional remarks or observations to make?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see it is 2.25 and we still have at least six items to discuss. As you see, we are having a lot of discussions here. So I think that we really will have to continue in the afternoon. The question I would like to put is to see whether we should resume at 4.00 or earlier. Half past three, I don't know if that would suit everyone, to have an hour's break and resume then. Otherwise, we'll be waiting for an hour and a half until 4.00. So I don't know. What do you think, Ms. Hollis? Let me consult the parties about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: We're prepared to proceed whenever you wish, Your Honours. Any time is fine with us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Even after a half-hour break?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our answer to that question is identical, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The same answer. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, are there any difficulties from the point of view of the registrar if we have a three-quarters-of-an-hour break and then resume?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The accused may need more time. They could use one hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The accused say that they have no need for any additional time, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then we're going to have a break of 45 minutes. We will resume at a quarter past three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated. We are now going to go on to the fourth item of the agenda, the defence of alibi. The question appears to have been raised by Mr. Zigic's Defence. The Chamber would like to know what exactly is entailed drawing the attention of the Defence counsel to the provisions of Article 67, paragraph A of the Rules. The Chamber is ready to discuss this matter now unless the parties wish to make additional written submissions or to have a separate hearing with the Defence counsel of Mr. Zigic. What is the exact position of the Defence counsel of Mr. Zigic regarding this matter? Who is going to take the floor, Mr. Tosic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my colleague, Mr. Stojanovic, will be presenting our views in respect of this matter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you. Then, Mr. Stojanovic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. The Defence of Mr. Zigic unfortunately has only recently heard about and been told that it will be using this defence during this trial, and I think that we informed our learned colleagues of the Prosecution within a reasonable time span, and we hope that that is all right and is -- will not leave the Prosecution without the possibility and the necessary time to prepare for this kind of defence, and it is the defence of alibi only with respect to one event. And we have submitted a letter to Ms. Hollis in which we state specifically what counts of the indictment we refer to and the methods for our defence. It is the Keraterm event. We have still not arrived at that, and we don't know if we will be robbing the Prosecution of their valuable time by stressing this now. On the other hand, collecting evidence and proof for this type of event is still an ongoing process. We have already got some witnesses, found some of them, but we are still searching for others. I should just like to request that if the discussion in this matter is extended, that it should not be in public session because in our letter, we name names, the names of witnesses to the letter -- in the letter to the Prosecution and we demand protective measures for those witnesses. We ask that they be protected witness. And I hope that the Prosecution will accept this manner of disclosure with the slight delay that exists but nonetheless, having said that -- it does come under Rule 67(B) and comply with that Rule and does not exclude the possibility of this type of defence even subsequently, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stojanovic, how do you see the situation in view of the provisions of Article 67 which says "as soon as possible" and, in any event, before the beginning of trial. You know that the trial started on the 28th of February. What is your response to this question?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I consider that you are completely correct in referring to that provision but I think that subrule B, subsection B of that same Rule does provide for that possibility and, on the other hand, we feel that this is not an unfair procedure as the opposite side in our view, and they are competent of assessing how long the testimony of their witnesses would last with respect to Keraterm and when they wish to begin that. But I don't think it is unfair and happily, because the testimony with respect to the events in Keraterm have not yet started. We have not yet heard testimony about Keraterm. Let us remind you that this is an alibi for an event that took place on the 24th of July. It says 2000, and that is an error here, it should state 1992. So the 24th of July 1992, that is the event. And I think that it is in the interests of justice for you to allow us to have certain witnesses state that Mr. Zigic at the relevant time, in the relevant period, was not at the scene of the crime and that they can confirm this through their testimony. So I think that the subsection B of the Rule does give scope to the Defence for this. Of course we are fully conscious of the fact that we have not fully complied with the provisions of the -- what you have just stipulated. Thank you. I apologise, but may I just say that perhaps we could hear the official stand of the opposite side. Of course, I never view them as the opposite side or party, but perhaps they can help us and state their views.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you very much, Mr. Stojanovic. We're going to hear the views of the Prosecutor. Ms. Hollis, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, we have received an initial notification that the Defence does intend to proceed with alibi as to that specific date, for the specific event that may have occurred in Keraterm on that date. We have also been given notice that this is a provisional notice that we have received from the Defence and that they have not yet been able to locate all potential witnesses on the alibi defence. Your Honours, we also note the language of the Rule that says that in any event prior to trial such notice may be given. That language aside, Your Honour, the Prosecution believes that, as we understand what the Defence has explained to us, we should have sufficient time to be able to deal with this defence. So at this point we would not rely on the plain language of the Rule and ask Your Honours to preclude the Defence. Should they come in at a much later date with a very long list of witnesses, perhaps we won't be able to meet it, but we're not in a position now to argue that you should deny them this defence. We would not argue that. We do note, Your Honour, that subsection (B) of the Rule does not give the party the right to proceed with other witnesses on it but indicates the accused may testify about it. But again we believe, at this point at least, that we would be able to adequately prepare for this defence. As I indicated, just to make it clear, our position could change depending on how much later we get the full notice and how many witnesses are involved, but for now we think we could prepare.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Ms. Hollis, are you able, at this point, to give us some approximation of -- if you did get -- the provisional notice became an absolute notice, say, within the next -- to the end of this month or within the next three weeks, along with a list of however many witnesses the Defence wanted to call, would that significantly expand the amount of time that you think you'd need to complete the Prosecution's whole case? And if so, by roughly -- it's hard to estimate but by some measure of how much?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: It's difficult to say in the abstract, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Yes, I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: -- but we think that in terms of our case in chief, that may not duly expand it. We anticipate that once we actually heard the alibi defence presented in the Defence case, that may expand a rebuttal case. But in terms of our case in chief, at this point we don't really think it would significantly expand it, and perhaps would not expand it at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stojanovic, have you any additional observations? What is the date that you envisage by which you would be able to submit this notification?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, our request comes together with a reservation. We know about one more witness who is in Germany, but we do not know his address.
