All the others we state here and we have their statements as well, and I think that that would be fair vis-à-vis the Prosecution to give them those -- supply them with those statements. So, Your Honours, as we have not complied with this on time, we will abide by your rulings and the opposite side. We could supply this information within the space of three days. We would welcome a longer period because of this one additional witness, but as I say, in the present situation we feel it to be our duty to comply with any decision that you reach, and in line with the Prosecution. The problem is actually just this one witness who is in Germany. He is a Muslim, according to our information, and that would require more time, for that one witness. But if we may, we would -- if it is not too much to ask, then by the end of next week. We would supply the Prosecution with this information by the end of next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that it would be proper to make a written motion about this, and the Chamber will make its ruling. Do you have any additional questions, Ms. Hollis, about what has just been said by Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, we can go on to the fifth item of the agenda, and that is request for an expert opinion, for a medical expert opinion, especially a psychiatric or psychological expert opinion, must be motivated and must allow the Judges to define as precisely as possible the mission to be entrusted -- the experts would be entrusted with. Regarding the latter, the Chamber would like to draw the attention of the parties to the provisions of the Rules regarding the possibility of designating such and such an expert, and specifically we are referring to Rule 78 [sic], and not 68, 78 bis, which says that it is important that the experts can appear as neutral as possible in the judicial process, strictly speaking. It would also be appropriate that requests for expert opinions should be used only for their specific purpose, and that is to inform the parties and the Judges regarding a specific technical point. Therefore, they should be distinguished from other motions which the parties may submit. The question is the following: Do you have any comments to make regarding this specific point? Ms. Hollis.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise, but what Rule did you refer us to? Perhaps I don't have the right book. Did you say Rule 78 bis?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 78 bis, yes. I apologise, 74 bis. I'm sorry, you are right. Thank you very much, Ms. Hollis, I made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we certainly would have no opposition to the Trial Chamber acting pursuant to this Rule. We would suggest that some type of showing would need to be made to a Trial Chamber to move forward and appoint such an expert, but it could perhaps best assist the Court by using this type of procedure, especially if the moving party envisions that based on the findings they will present a certain Defence or a certain position at trial so we would certainly have no objection to the Trial Chamber acting pursuant to this Rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Ms. Hollis. Are there any observations on the part of the Defence, any of the Defence or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No comments, Your Honour. We accept what has been said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Thank you very much. So we can go on to the sixth item, sixth and seventh. I think we should take them together, depositions by Presiding Officers and timetable. These questions are perhaps linked together as I just said. According to what has been announced, the Prosecutor should complete the presentation of evidence in its case in chief in 38 days. The Prosecutor lost three days for reasons we are well aware of. Therefore, 35 days of hearings remain. On this day, I think that the Prosecutor has used 11 and a half days of hearings and I wish to check this with the registrar. Madam Registrar, can you tell us how many days the Prosecution has used so far?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: So far they used 2566 minutes. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Oh my God.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's very precise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: How many seconds?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe we should multiply by 60. 120.000, so how many days is that?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 12 days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is a little more than I estimated. I forget some minutes yesterday and then today also, so 12 days, 12 and a half days. About 23 days are left or 24 and a half -- no, 22 and a half. So that is less than five weeks of hearings. I turn now to the Office of the Prosecutor to ask Ms. Hollis in view of the witnesses that you have already called and the decision of the Chamber regarding judicial notice. Can you tell us how we stand, Ms. Hollis?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, first of all we disagree with those figures as to 12 days. I didn't have sufficient mathematical ability to go to medical school --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Minutes or seconds?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, it's more like ten days. And also, Your Honour, I would ask if the days when we were appropriately in Status Conferences are being used in that computation as well so I'm not sure that we would agree with those number of days. But that aside, let me tell you where we think we are in terms of our evidence. We were looking at our evidence yesterday and our witness list as a result of a recent decision of the Trial Chamber and in terms of our deposition witnesses that we had listed, at least four of those witnesses will not be called, and we believe it's very likely that we would not depose any of those witnesses. But certainly in terms of in our list of 28 April under deposition witnesses, number three, number four, number five and number six would not be called. And we're looking at whether we would need to depose number one and number two. At this point we think probably we would not depose them. Now, in terms of the remainder of the case, we've also looked at our witness list with the decision in mind and based on our calculations, we believe that as of this time, we would have 96 hours of witness testimony. That is if we do not have to call experts on proof of death. Now, if we were to have to call experts on proof of death, it would be our intention to put the experts on and present their statements to the court and not carry them through a direct examination. So in terms of additional time for direct examination of these experts, that would be limited to the time it would take them basically to authenticate their report. And, again, we don't know what the posture of their evidence would be towards the end. We may not have to call proof of death expert witness testimony at all. Your Honour, in regard to the time and the estimates for our witnesses, we certainly do not contest in any way losing the three days, that's not what I'm about to talk about, but perhaps we misunderstand the use of these estimates because we realise and we've been very mindful that we have got over our estimates, but our understanding is that our estimates are only for direct examination. They do not include cross-examination. So when we give the number of hours we think is necessary in these estimates, it's for direct examination. So if we're counting the number of days we're in court, that's a bit misleading as well because that includes cross-examination of the witnesses. So perhaps we need to look at this and refine our numbers a little better. But as we believe now, we would take approximately 96 hours in court to put on the rest of our case with the proviso I gave about expert witnesses for proof of death.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And without cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That's based on adding up our estimates. Now, we believe in any trial as we go along and we see the evidentiary posture, it's possible to further refine our witness list and drop witnesses out. But to ensure that we give you a full picture and basically a worst-case scenario, that is what we're giving you, 96 hours. And if we have misunderstood the estimates, please let us know that, but our understanding is that these are estimates of our time on direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: If I might ask, have you been able -- you may not have made this calculation, but based on the experience so far, have you been able to make any correlation between the time that you estimated or even the real time that your direct did and the time for cross? I know is varies between witnesses, but on average.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: You know, Your Honour, we haven't. The Prosecution has been very observant and very appreciative of the Defence approach to cross-examination. We believe that it's been very direct and certainly not unduly long at all, but in terms of a correlation we haven't been able to make one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Hollis. I think we have to reassess the situation, yes. Perhaps I could make this suggestion to you, we will study the matter within the Chamber and we will tell Mr. Olivier Fourmy to get in touch with you to have a more precise calculation. Perhaps that is the best way to deal with this matter. Are you in agreement with that, Ms. Hollis?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: We would appreciate that, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Are there any comments on the part of the Defence? No comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No comments, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much. I should like to remind you that we will have at least eight days of hearings in July and that we will resume our hearings of this case on the 28th of August; that is just so that you should be informed. But as I have said, we will make our own estimation. We are going to communicate through the legal officer with Ms. Hollis to see whether our estimates coincide or not, and after that we will inform the parties. In any event, there is one other matter which perhaps needs to be taken up, and that is the question of depositions by Presiding Officers. I have the impression that the witnesses that the Prosecutor has put on his list for depositions were witnesses who should testify about historical circumstances, et cetera, et cetera. I don't know whether the Prosecutor wishes to abide by this, taking into account the question of judicial notice. How do we stand in regard to this question of deposition statements?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. In regard to deposition witnesses for the Prosecution, we will definitely not call the last four that are listed; we will not take depositions from them. We are evaluating whether we need to depose the first two witnesses and have not reached a final decision, but it appears that we would not be deposing them either. So at most we would depose two, and probably we will depose none.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So when the legal officer talks to you, Ms. Hollis, perhaps, if you have a final opinion by then, you could let us know so that we can organise ourselves. Do you agree, Ms. Hollis?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you agree and do you accept? I must be very precise.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: I make an informed, voluntary acceptance of that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Ms. Hollis. Thank you. So regarding the Defence, still on the question of deposition witnesses, I had the impression that perhaps those depositions could occur sometime between the end of the Prosecution case and the beginning of the Defence case. I would like to know what comments the Defence would have. We're still rather far from that issue, I know it is early to talk about the preparation of the Defence, but I know that there may be a certain anxiety on the part of the Defence regarding the cross-examination, and I wish to remind you that you have your own case to present your defence evidence and that we will have a Pre-Defence Conference. I wish to remind you of that. But I would like to see your reactions in relation to this idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I speak in my own name alone. When we discussed depositions of witnesses, as you know, it was a different Trial Chamber and a different situation, and the Defence was guided in bringing its decision that the depositions had two facts to contend with: first of all, time, because the trial was not even envisaged and we wanted to do what we could before the start of trial to shorten the time of the trial itself; and secondly, in the Republika Srpska, the Defence really does have a problem with the witnesses who would be ready to come and testify before this Tribunal. So that quite simply we had to compromise, and, therefore, the Defence of Mr. Kvocka gave you a larger number of names for witnesses, deposition witnesses. But we shall do our utmost that by the time of trial, the Defence case, we shall try to revise the list and to bring as many witnesses to the courtroom as possible. What we won't be able to do in court we shall have to do on the basis of the other method. But I do think it is a good idea to have this take place after the Prosecution case and before the Defence case, if there are any new witnesses to contend with. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Very well, Mr. Simic. Mr. Nikolic, do you have any response?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no special reaction. All I can say is that this Defence team is very much interested in having testimony by deposition, but it is not in the same position as the Prosecution or Mr. Kvocka's Defence team to reduce the number of witnesses for depositions. The number remains constant because we are dealing with certain individuals who are vital for the defence of our accused, and so this Defence team would like to stay with that number. Of course, as regards time, we fully agree with the proposal Your Honour has just given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Nikolic. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I completely concur with what you have said and with what my colleagues have said before me. I accept a parallel system as well. Because there are enough of us, one person could be in Banja Luka while another one is here in the courtroom, and that evidence could be presented and depositions presented in parallel form which would speed up the whole procedure. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Fila. Mr. Tosic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we agree with respect to your position regarding the depositions in the period after the Prosecution case and before the Defence case gets going. But I cannot accept and do not agree with the position of my colleague Mr. Fila with respect to the fact that the depositions be taken specifically in Banja Luka, for example, and to follow the proceedings in this courtroom at the same time, this parallelism. So much from me. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much. Mr. Jovan Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we agree with your proposal and your observations. As to the number of witnesses, at this point in time we are still not able to give you an exact number. We have handed in the statements that we have collected. We entered into these proceedings a little late, but we do hope that in the course of the coming month we will come up with a definite list of witnesses who will be heard by deposition, and those to be heard in this courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you, Mr. Jovan Simic. Ms. Hollis, have you any additional observations to make? I'm sorry. Before that, I think Mr. Nikolic has something to add.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise for taking the floor and reacting a little late. But in view of the fact, Your Honour, that you have heard the positions of the individual Defence teams, when you bring in your ruling, I should like to ask you to bear in mind what the majority has proposed, because for my part, I can say that I do not agree that we work in parallel form, as proposed by Mr. Fila, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we will bear all that in mind. Thank you, in any event, for drawing our attention to this. Ms. Hollis now. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, the Prosecution's position remains the same in regard to Defence witnesses. Those we have agreed to take by deposition we still agree to take by deposition. New witnesses that are proposed by deposition we will evaluate, just as we evaluated those previously. We would, for the record, Your Honours, reiterate our position that for Defence witnesses who are unwilling to come to the Tribunal, that either videolink testimony from an area they are willing to appear would be acceptable or the Prosecution does agree that, if needed, depositions taken in the areas where they are willing to appear would also be in the interests of justice. We have stated in the past that we believe it's possible to depose witnesses in Banja Luka, if that's what's necessary, and to the extent the Defence believes they need that for their witnesses, then we would support their request in that regard. We would find it difficult to have a parallel structure such as was proposed, but that is more for Your Honours to evaluate than for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should also like to consult the parties regarding a possible modification of the management of time that we have done so far. As you know, we have adopted this system of working during the day with two half-hour breaks. We did this also in the interests of the accused because we know that if we have a pause shorter than half an hour the accused cannot leave the courtroom. But they also need to have a rest to be able to follow the debates fully. In the meantime, we talked amongst ourselves about this and we received many suggestions and a lot of feedback, if I can call it that, and we were about to modify slightly the organisation of time so as to have a half-hour break the first break, and then the second break of one hour; that is, we could begin at 9.20 in the morning and finish around, and I say "around," 3.00. It could be a quarter to three. The point is that, as you know, there are certain habits with regard to meals and there are many people who like to have a longer break for lunch. So to meet these requests, one -- we do have a half-hour break first and then an hour-long break after that. I would like to hear your reactions. As I have said, the Chamber will take its decisions, but with an explanation, and we would like to consult the parties. And I would also like to say that this Chamber has a very busy schedule because, as you know, it is working on two cases simultaneously and it is working every day every week. And if it appears to the public that this Chamber works only from 9.30 until 2.30 and the other Chamber from 9.30 until 4.00 or 4.30, it may appear that the other Chamber is working harder than this one. I'm not interested in any comparisons. I'm just saying that we have the same hours of hearings but in the mornings we have the hearings, as you know, to make sure that the witnesses who are present are heard and we have, in the afternoons, our status meetings our meetings and our discussions. It's a different manner of organising the time and managing the time. So I can understand that very often it is very hard to spend all this time in the courtroom without having a rest because I'm telling you now, you have breaks, but we have none because when we're not working on Kvocka, we have another case, and we see other teams of the Prosecution and the Defence, but the Judges are the same. So perhaps we should review a little the organisation of time so as to really give a chance to everyone do have a slightly longer break, to have a normal meal, because we are human beings, as you know, we're not machines. Regarding this matter of modifying our working hours by beginning at 9.20 and ending more or less at 3.00 or quarter to three with a half-hour break first, and second hour-long break, what is your opinion, Ms. Hollis? Would that suit you or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the Prosecution likes to have one meal a day, whether we need it or not, so that would suit us and, of course, we appreciate being able to be in court as long as possible so we would think that would be very fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We see that the Prosecutors are also human beings. Let's see what the Defence has to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll see at the end of the case whether they are human beings but in any event, the Defence agrees with this proposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And do you need to eat only at the end of the trial or already now?

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I had something else in mind, and I'm sure you know what I meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. So now another question. That is the outstanding agenda item. I don't know whether Ms. Hollis has any other matters to address at this Status Conference.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honour, we do. We have one issue we would like to put on the record, and that has to do Your Honour with confronting witnesses with potential impeachment or contradiction matters. We noted yesterday in the questions by Defence counsel for accused, Kvocka, that Defence counsel, it appeared, was about to confront the witness with a statement and potentially with contradictions or inconsistencies in the statement. Because of this whole issue about the use of statements, that was deferred, but the Prosecution would like to put on the record that it is the Prosecution's view that both parties are bound to put to each witness matters of impeachment they wish to raise and areas of contradiction that they wish to raise. We believe that the Rule contemplates that and I believe that that is, Your Honours, Rule 89(H). We also believe that the unique circumstances of this Tribunal requires that because if it doesn't happen, then the party who initially called the witness is faced with bringing them back from all over the world to address these issues. So we simply wanted to put on the record that we believe each party has an obligation to confront these witnesses with issues of impeachment and issues of contradiction while the witness is here. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Let me just clarify one thing. I certainly understand that in prior inconsistent statements and that confused me yesterday too. But are you suggesting that suppose a witness, your witness, is on direct and cross-examined, et cetera, sits down, and then when the Defence puts on its case two months from now, it brings forth a witness who contradicts in that witness' testimony what your prior witness. Are you suggesting that they had some obligation to give advance notice somehow to the first witness that that might happen?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, what we're -- what we are submitting is that whichever party it is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: -- has an obligation to put to the witness, "Isn't it true that, in fact, you told so and so something different," or "Isn't it true this and that," so that the witness, if it is that the witness said something different to someone else, that the witness has the opportunity to respond to that in this appearance rather than having to be called back. So that's the nature of the type of evidence we're talking about, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. I just wanted to understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Do you think we can really put hard and fast rules in this area?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we don't think you can put hard and fast rules but we believe that you can put a general rule. And in fact I misspoke, I believe it's not Rule 89(H) it's rule 90(H), 90(H). And the Prosecution submits that that is what this Rule is aimed at, and that is, to the greatest extent possible, put to the witness while they're here. If there are items of contradiction that the witness may later be recalled to explain, because otherwise these cases will go on. It's a matter of timeliness of the proceedings. It's a matter of not bringing witnesses back at great expense. It's not a matter of bringing witnesses back to retraumatise them by having to reappear before the Tribunal. But in terms of an absolute rule that is always the same, we understand that it could vary from case to case, but we believe as a general proposition, yes, it should be a general proposition and is what is intended by Rule 90(H).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Ms. Hollis. Has the Defence any comments to make regarding this point that has just been raised by Ms. Hollis?

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, perhaps precisely this question links -- is linked up with what I spoke about with respect to the proceedings, and then we could touch on that question and -- with what I wanted to see, the obligation of the Prosecution to present us with that, and I speak only in my own name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps you wish us to deal with this question first and then later on, Mr. Simic, you will have your question. Very well. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: The only comment I have is this, Your Honours, under Rule 90(H), you will see 90(H)(i) or 90(H)(ii). (H)(i) refers to cross-examination and matters of credibility specifically uses the word "credibility" and two refers to contradictions of the evidence. And if I understand what the point Ms. Hollis is making, indeed, it goes to the effectiveness of a cross-examination. If, during the cross-examination, a party is trying to bring out inconsistencies which go to credibility or contradictions which go to credibility and weight, clearly that is one of the reasons or purposes of cross-examination. So it really is a matter for counsel to effectively cross-examine in those regards. And that, to me, is the matter as I believe Judge Riad is suggesting, there's no hard and fast rule, but it's a matter for Your Honours to see what arises out of the testimony in its entirety including the cross-examination. That's all I have to say on that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. O'Sullivan. Are there any other comments regarding this matter? No? Very well. I take advantage of this opportunity, nevertheless, to say that the Chamber, I don't know how I should call this, but the discussions that we have had in the course of several Status Conferences, and we were -- we intended to supply you some kind of practical instructions by the Chamber which are the Chamber's interpretation of the Rules after the discussions that we have had, and I don't know whether that could be useful, but in any event, we're working on this working document, and I think it could be useful especially with regard to this point raised. There are many matters that we have agreed on, many that we have discussed, and the Chamber wishes to share with you some guidance as regards the practice of the Chamber, but we will see whether that will be useful for you or not. We have almost finished the document. We would like to supply you with it, and then we will see whether it can be a tool, a useful instrument for all of us. So now, Mr. Krstan Simic, the question you want to address.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this question, in a way, was opened by Mr. Nikolic but he didn't elaborate because it was neither the time or the place, and I would like to raise this problem and I'm sure that by solving the problem, effectively, we can speed up the trial process and avoid many misunderstandings which we have had so far, and I'll try to show this and demonstrate this by way of an example. We have the indictment to start off with, and all the Defence teams had objections to the form of the indictment. At that time, the Trial Chamber accepted the objections made by the Defence counsels and considered that the indictment was not precise enough and specific enough linked to the events, the time of the occurrences. The Victims and Witnesses Unit on the 12th of April, 1999, issued and order to the Prosecution to determine more specifically to amend the indictment in that sense. And the Prosecution on the 31st of May of that same year sent a document, an addendum to the indictment in which it gives more specifics and located the casualties and the perpetrators for whom it considered that they could prove this kind of treatment took place. We did not consider at the time that this was sufficient, but we accepted it in waiting for the trial to begin, and we thought that later on in practice, the rules and regulations would help us to resolve the situation. And in that sense, I should like to indicate Rule 65 ter (E)(iv), which provides for the fact that the Prosecution, in its submission, in keeping with Rule 73 bis is duty-bound to send a list of witnesses and under C, it states the points in the indictment as to which each witness will testify, including specific references to counts and relevant paragraphs in the indictment. The Prosecution did, indeed, send us a submission of that kind, we received it, but I seem to feel that in practice, that submission is not being applied and, quite simply, we are deviating from it and using up a lot of time and energy. In order to show this in practical terms, I shall quote the example for one particular witness whose testimony we have heard. It was Witness AJ. As it was a protected witness, those were his initials. Through this witness, the Prosecution wanted to prove Counts 1 to 3 of the indictment connected to C and D of the accused. This witness was not put forward at all as a witness to bear out any of these facts, any facts which relate to Mr. Kvocka, that is, in the indictment; however, the practice was quite different. We discussed this at greater length, whereas for all practical purposes we could have prepared ourselves for this witness. Very frequently witnesses don't seem to remember and they say that time has played its hand, and this is something of concern to the Defence counsel, that the witnesses, after two or three days of discussion with the Prosecution teams -- you know that two or three days is a long time because you know what can be said in two or three hours -- and then they said, "Well, we didn't remember that; we weren't asked that," and this can lead to misunderstandings. Because some of the witnesses spoke about events that were not the subject of their statements, and this led us to a position where we had Mirsad Alisic, a witness who is not a protected witness so I can state his name, he testified, we had his statement, and after his testimony, we found ourselves faced with the following situation: Neither in the testimony, nor during the examination-in-chief or the statement or during the cross-examination, did he make mention of a fact which he mentioned in response to a question asked by Judge Wald. So that is something which causes concern to us, and there are many examples of that kind. Let me mention another witness. Edin Mrkalj, we heard his testimony here recently. Mr. Mrkalj, his statement, for example, was taken after the confirmation of the indictment against Mr. Kvocka. It was taken by the same Prosecution team representing the indictment, and new points cropped up. We reacted and Ms. Hollis said -- in fact, things were mentioned that did not exist in the minutes. Therefore, I would like to propose and suggest, if I have the competency to do so -- and I think that in practice this could be realised -- that the Prosecution should stick to its submission in calling out the witnesses. And this would facilitate all of us in this trial, especially you the Judges, that the witnesses are being called to talk about such and such a paragraph of the indictment, and that in our cross-examination we should adhere to what is provided for by Rule 65, I think it is, 65 ter, because that is the duty of the Prosecution as well. I think we should gain efficiency, and we would avoid any nervousness, any surprises, we would not tax the witness too much, and I think this would be to the advantage of a fair trial. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Krstan Simic. Madam Hollis, I think you have many things to respond to now.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, in regards to Rule 65 ter, we suggest that is a Rule for the Pre-Trial Judge in managing the case for trial, and that what is provided for the Pre-Trial Judge should not limit what is produced at trial. We suggest that the real core of this issue is really adequate notice to the Defence, and if the Defence feels it has not received adequate notice, then we suggest that the proper remedy is to raise that point with Your Honours to determine what additional time may be necessary to cross-examine the witness on this point, or what other remedies may be appropriate. We don't believe that the appropriate remedy is to limit witnesses to what is put forward in a document that is for the use of the Pre-Trial Judge in determining how much for trial and such matters as that. We would again point, Your Honour, to the reality of this Tribunal, and that is that when statements are taken from witnesses, in many instances they are not taken for the case that is currently before this Tribunal. Even after one indictment has been confirmed, statements may be taken in regard to a different case. In fact, for Mr. Mrkalj, the statement was taken in regard to the Tadic proceedings. It was not taken in view of these accused because these accused were not in custody, nor did we have any indication they would be in custody at any time in the near future. So the system is very different than it is in many jurisdictions, where a statement is taken from a witness for one specific case and that is the purpose for which it is later used. Statements that are taken by the Office of the Prosecutor very often have to do with crimes that were committed throughout a camp or throughout an opstina or throughout a region, so that they do not focus on particular accused. For that reason, these statements can't be seen -- the contents of the statements can't be seen as everything the witness knows that may become relevant in later cases. So we do have a difference there. We suggest it comes down to notice and how we deal with that. The way the Prosecution is attempting to deal with that when it gets notice early enough is to provide the Defence counsel with proffers that would include new relevant information. There are instances where the information is obtained just prior to the witness testifying so that even a proffer would not solve the notice requirement. We believe, again, the issue is notice and how we deal with lack of notice when that is raised by the Defence, and we do not believe that 65 ter should limit the evidence that comes forward in trial. Again, we believe that the underlying issue for admissibility of evidence is is it relevant and is it probative. Another consideration is has the Defence been given sufficient notice of the evidence. But we think restricting either side to what may come forward in 65 ter, as a general rule, would not advance the interests of justice and would result in this Chamber being denied the use of relevant and probative evidence. So, again, we believe the real issue is how do we deal with lack of notice or untimely notice, and that is how we would respond to Defence counsel's submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Have you got an idea of what adequate notice would be, then?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we think it would depend upon, really, the type of information they receive. If it is information that is consistent with other evidence in the case, that is consistent with the approach that the Prosecution is taking, then perhaps less notice would be required. If it is something that is totally new, is inconsistent with all the other evidence in the case, then there would be a real element of surprise and additional time would be required. But again we believe you'd have to look at this in terms of the specific evidence that we were talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Hollis, I'm viewing this question within the context of the totality of the discussions we have had here, all these prior statements, et cetera. Could it not be a good solution to respond to this suggestion made by Mr. Krstan Simic just now? That is, perhaps it would be useful to focus the debate properly, to focus the examination-in-chief and the cross-examination, to say before the examination-in-chief begins -- and I don't think that would cost you much because you have investigated so much work anyway -- "Here we have this witness who is going to testify about such and such events or counts in the indictment," with a specific reference to the appropriate paragraph in the indictment. I'm reading from the Rules. I think this could assist the Defence a great deal, and when you have statements of witnesses, and I understand they were taken so as to be used for this case or another case, there are many things perhaps which are not really focused on this particular case. I think that the suggestion of Mr. Krstan Simic could perhaps be of assistance. Are you capable of responding to that suggestion, Ms. Hollis?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Perhaps I misunderstood the suggestion of Mr. Simic. My understanding was his suggestion was we had to stay with whatever was set forward in 65 ter. That, I disagree with. Your Honour's suggestion that before a witness testifies we indicate what the witness will testify about is something that I believe we could do with more exactitude, but this would be prior to the witness' testimony. I would distinguish that from us being bound by what was set forward in the 65 ter submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, because Rule 64 ter is for the pre-trial stage, and we are not in that stage now. But I think you have done this work for the pre-trial, so I think it could be useful, as far as I have been able to see from the Defence, that before beginning the testimony, one could say, "We are calling this witness to talk about this, this, and this." Could you do that, Ms. Hollis?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that we could do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Krstan Simic, have you any response?

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A very brief comment. Clearly Ms. Hollis and I have not understood one another completely. Ms. Hollis has confirmed indirectly everything I have said. When mentioning Mr. Mrkalj, Ms. Hollis said, "We took that statement for the Tadic case." The statement from the Tadic case, which was disclosed to the Defence, a witness is brought in to talk about the Kvocka case. We don't have his statement. We learn here for the first time things from his testimony. Out of respect for the Chamber, we didn't ask for the trial to be suspended, we didn't say that Mrkalj's statement had been disclosed. Ms. Hollis has just admitted that. We need new time of a month or so. Where would that take us? I don't think that's a big problem since the Prosecution has submitted its amendments to the indictment, and it says specifically Witness AJ will be heard regarding Counts such and so, charges such and such. We just wished the Prosecution document to be implemented rather than this list being expanded endlessly. It was the Prosecution who specified what AJ would be testifying about, and they said that they would be proving Counts 1 to 3 in relation to the accused Radic, C and D, and Zigic. So we simply wish what they submitted to the Trial Chamber as their suggestion, as their decision, to be put into practice. No additional submissions, only the implementation of what we had expected the Prosecution to implement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope you will allow me to say a few words, as colleague Simic mentioned my name when he started to elaborate this point. I just wish to say that the Defence was, in a sense, handicapped in conceiving the strategy of defence, because our defence strategy was based on the submission of the Prosecution, and that is how we viewed witness statements and that is how they prepared for the cross. Because the witness that colleague Simic has just mentioned had nothing to do with our client, according to -- and this, according to the submission of the Prosecution itself. So our strategy was based on the statements of those witnesses that the Prosecution would say would be proving the charges against the accused Kos. When the trial started, things changed. I did react at a certain point, through an objection. However, I was told that the indictment provided the scope. Yes, but at the time I had in mind the ruling of the previous Trial Chamber which asked the Prosecution to be more specific -- make the amendment more specific and which it did. It was more specific, making different chapters, A, B, C, D, regarding victims and accountability. So this is just to add to what my learned friend, Mr. Simic, has just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In any event, I think there are certain new elements -- thank you, Mr. Nikolic -- there are certain new elements in what Mr. Nikolic has said. So are you going to respond, Ms. Hollis?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe the basic point that is being raised is the same point, and that has to do with notice. In terms of making the indictment more specific, that was done, that was accepted by the Trial Chamber, so we don't think that that is an open issue. So again we think it comes back to notice, and I would rely on the comments I had made earlier about notice and note again that in terms of what Your Honour is suggesting, the Prosecution understands that to be different than what Defence counsel for accused Kvocka is suggesting. It is your suggestion that we believe that we could comply with, and we do not believe that the 65 ter submission should be restrictively applied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krstan Simic, have you any further comments or have you finished?

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have finished, but this would go on endlessly. Rule 65 ter is part of the trial. It gives a guideline for the trial. It simply says so many conditions need to be fulfilled for the trial to begin and then we come to briefs, and we will abide by what we have said in those briefs, I promise you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much. Are there any questions to deal with, to address? I am putting the question to you all. Yes, maybe Mr. Tosic. Thank you, Mr. Tosic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have one question that will be expanded by my colleague, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead, Mr. Stojanovic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Let me remind the Trial Chamber that in the past week, we have already informed the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution that we cannot collect all the material in evidence we need for the Defence of Mr. Zigic. We are talking about photographs, the photographs of precise individuals. I cannot tell you which individuals not to have to go into private session. The Defence considers that there is -- that the identity of these individuals has been changed and with respect to the charges against Mr. Zigic, and some witnesses, Prosecution witnesses, have described Zigic as being precisely those people on the photographs that we are seeking, looking for. And some of the witnesses we have heard also confirm that it was not Zigic, but that according to the descriptions, they were descriptions of other persons whose photographs we are looking for. But in addition to the numerous personal contacts that we have had and the written submissions we have tabled requests to the highest authorities in Republika Srpska, the Ministry of Defence, the municipal organs and so on and so forth, the Ministry of the Interior, et cetera, but all this has not come up with any result. On the other hand, the Prosecution, according to our request, has endeavoured to search its archives and help the Defence but, unfortunately, they don't seem to have been able to come up with anything. The Tribunal, through this Trial Chamber, does have the authority in conformity with Rule 29(2)(a) and (c) of the Statute to make it incumbent upon Republika Srpska or Bosnia-Herzegovina to hand over certain documents, and the application of those competencies has been further elaborated in Rule, I think it is, 54 bis. However, quite obviously, it would mean the application of an unwieldy process and institution which would imply the possibility of complaints from us, appeals from us, and the interested state which would mean an instrument which could, for a time, burden and even disturb the regular course of the trial itself. Therefore, the Defence has done its best to -- as this was a last resort, we wanted to avoid that particular instrument and try and come by what it is searching for in a roundabout way, and a shorter way. And we have had contact, direct contacts with Mr. Jovicic in the past week. He is the liaison officer of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina with this Tribunal, and he has promised to help us; he has promised his assistance in this matter. I think that that assistance would gain more weight if this Trial Chamber were to give us a signal and to lend its support to us for this kind of cooperation, to give the go ahead. I think that's a pre-requisite which would bear fruit, and that we would reach our goal in that way. The other thing that would be of great assistance to us would be if the Prosecution could change the order of the witnesses, certain witnesses, Fadil Abdagic being one of them, and Omer Mecin [phoen] and Asmir Mesic. And if we could hear Witness T again, and we've already discussed that matter on a previous occasion. I think that it is a request to arrive at something that -- which can be beneficial to all of us. And provoked by some witness testimonies, I'm not going to mention them now, but shortly we're going to have a situation where one of them will perhaps say, as he had said in his written statement, that Zoran Zigic killed such and such an individual, but after that, we come to a description of Zoran Zigic. That he is a high man, a blond man with a earring in his ear, et cetera. So what we are trying to do is to take a shortcut in arriving at what we consider to be crucial for our Defence case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stojanovic, I think that we have already said that a written request should be made because elements of identification are in question. Is there anything new since then or is the situation the same as it was then?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. We merely tried to present the Court with this possibility and not be a binding order to a state which entails repercussions and consequences which will be unwieldy to this trial, but to have another form of assistance there from the Tribunal to have cooperation with the liaison officer, and understanding from the Prosecution with regarding to the order in which certain witnesses will be heard and examined. So we're doing our utmost to avoid anything that would make the trial unwieldy and prolong it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but I don't know exactly what we can do to give content to this support. What would you like me to do? I make a phone call to someone to tell them, "We support the position of Mr. Stojanovic." What, exactly, are you asking for? That is my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, with the liaison officer, he would like encouragement from the Tribunal for cooperation with the Defence and, of course, with the Prosecution following requests linked to preparations for the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but I can't do that. I cannot pick up the telephone and say to the representative in Bosnia-Herzegovina, "We sympathise with the question raised by Mr. Stojanovic, can you give it to him?" That is not how things are done. Either you make a motion in line with Article 29 and the Chamber will make a decision, or you don't make a motion and the Chamber will wait. The Chamber does not take -- give support to any party. We, as a Chamber, we do support your position and your quest for the truth and, the Chamber will do everything to establish the truth but, as you know, there are mechanisms for doing so. Either you make a motion or you don't submit a motion. There is no half-way solution. I have to be quite frank with you, Mr. Stojanovic. As I said, I cannot telephone a representative of Bosnia-Herzegovina or Republika Srpska to say, "Look, you have to do such and such a thing." That's something I cannot do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you, Your Honour. I think we will table a written submission in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Hollis, do you have any comments to make regarding this matter?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think now it's Mr. Jovan Simic's turn.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I should like to raise two short questions and add something after that. I'm not quite clear, perhaps I understood it incorrectly, but you said in July we would have at least eight days of trial. Does that mean that there is the possibility of prolonging that period or are we only going to have eight days? This is very vital to our team so that we can reserve our tickets, flight tickets, hotels and so on. And my second question relates to August. You said that the trial goes ahead on the 28th of August but don't know how long it will continue. The same problem exists because of our accommodation arrangements, travel arrangements and so on, thank you. And the third point that I wish to raise is the question of the transport of my client, Mr. Prcac, which has still not -- a method which has still not been solved. According to my information given from Ms. Hollis, there are two requests. The first was from 1999 requesting that all the accused, individually, that is to say, be transported separately and individually. In keeping with that, a request was made that Mr. Prcac cannot be transported together with them. I'm referring to the situation with the detention unit and the trip to and from the Tribunal, and the situation is as follows: The four accused do go together, they are transported together which the registrar has enabled in a very good way and a speedy way. Their transport has been organised in a speedy fashion, but Mr. Prcac has to wait. And as Mr. Prcac has a high blood pressure problem and health problems generally, he also has a serious headache problem, and he is the oldest of the accused, and I would like to avoid that his health situation becomes even worse and that he is not able to continue the trial. That is one point. Secondly, I asked Ms. Hollis, having spoken to Mr. Rhodes, if possible, that she withdraw her request so that all the accused would come and go to the Tribunal together, be transported together. She told me that if the request of that kind exists, then that she will ask that each of the accused be taken separately but that she would have nothing against all of them going together. I should now like to ask the Trial Chamber, because I am between the secretariat and the Prosecution, I find myself placed in the middle and cannot solve this. Could we see how this matter can be settled so that it can indeed be settled and may not have to take up more time of this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Jovan Simic. It is, of course, not up to the Chamber to deal with this question. The only thing that the Chamber can do is mention the matter to the Registry. I think we did that already, but I don't know whether Madam Registrar was here at the time. Do you have any feedback regarding this matter, Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I already checked with Mr. Rhodes, and he suggest to me that actually we should have to wait for the request from the Prosecutor in this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor, you said?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, because the Prosecutor, they are lodging the request in March requesting sending all these accused back to the detention centre individually. So if you want to put them together, send them in one vehicle, then you have to send -- lodging another request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't want anything because I cannot want. But in any event, before giving the floor to Ms. Hollis, the fact that I have here regarding eight days in July and the resumption on the 28th of August are the data I have before me. If you need additional information, perhaps you could talk to Mr. Olivier Fourmy, he is here. Perhaps he could give us more details regarding the calendar. As for the transportation of the accused, and specifically of Mr. Prcac, can you tell us anything, Ms. Hollis? The registrar tells us that the Registry is wait for a request from the Prosecutor. I thought they were waiting for a request from Mr. Jovan Simic, so I don't understand anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not quite sure that they are waiting for, but I can tell you this, the Prosecution in the past has requested through the registrar certain no-contact orders without supervision involving these accused. Those orders have been acted upon and no contact has been ordered, absent supervision. The Prosecution has never asked anyone to transport people individually or in a group. Our request has been for no contact without supervision, and those decisions have been made by the Registry to allow that involving these accused. The Prosecution certainly is in accord with Defence counsel for Mr. Prcac, that Mr. Prcac's health must be taken into account. The Registry has been able to, in its view, comply with the no-contact orders and to transport four of these five accused together. The Prosecution doesn't understand why -- if it believes it can comply with the no-contact orders and transport four together, they can't transport five together. So we have no position on that at all. We simply have said, made a request that there be no contact among these accused without supervision. How the Registry carries that out is up to the Registry and how it transports people is up to the Registry. So the Prosecution is also at a loss as to what we are to request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Jovan Simic. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I just wondered if it's possible, with an impasse, like a bureaucratic impasse like this, even if somebody can just sent them a copy of the transcript of what we've just said here so that we know that you are not directly -- that you are in no way opposing this, maybe we could get over this bureaucratic hurdle.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Indeed, and we've made it known to Registry personnel in the courtroom that we are not opposed to this happening if there is supervision, and we are not opposed to adequate measures being taken regarding Mr. Prcac's health. So we will do that again if it assists the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now Mr. Jovan Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the only thing we are asking the Registrar to do is a written submission of any kind on the subject, as expounded by Ms. Hollis. We're losing time talking about it. All they need -- Mr. Rhodes said, "I'll organise it. All I need is a written request by the Prosecution or an agreement on the part of the Prosecution." Nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the transcript of the hearing should be sufficient. Madam Registrar, could you send this part of the transcript -- because after all, the hearing is public -- to the Registry so that they know there is no opposition on the part of the Prosecution to this?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: May I please also refer to Rule 66? Maybe perhaps it helps you. We need a written request from the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, we are not going to continue this debate. You will take note of the position taken, Madam Registrar, so that things be resolved, and the Chamber is going to check. This, I can do. But regarding Mr. Stojanovic's question, I can do nothing. So I think there are no further matters to deal with, at least for a few days we will not be having other matters. We have dealt with all the outstanding issues, so we will meet here again to resume our case. The hearing is adjourned, a hearing that was extremely productive, and we will see its effect in practice in the future. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: adjourned at 4.57 p.m.
